title: 2 Samuel 23:8–17
context: A list of David’s mighty men begins with the Three, Josheb Basshebeth, Eleazar, and Shammah, whose single-handed stands against the Philistines are credited to the LORD’s victory. Three of the thirty break through the Philistine lines to bring David water from Bethlehem’s well, and David pours it out to the LORD rather than drink what cost their lives. Both traditions read this as shared ground on courage, loyalty, and reverence, and several names and numbers differ from the parallel in 1 Chronicles 11.

verses.text: These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb Basshebeth, a Tahchemonite, chief of the captains; he was called Adino the Eznite, who killed eight hundred at one time.
verses.arminianNotes:
The list opens with Josheb Basshebeth, chief of the captains, who killed eight hundred at one time. Arminian readers note that the narrator honors faithful service and courage.

The parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:11 names him Jashobeam and gives three hundred; the name and number variants are textual issues interpreters discuss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God raising up faithful men around his anointed king.

The phrase “he was called Adino the Eznite” is obscure in Hebrew. These textual differences are noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: After him was Eleazar the son of Dodai the son of an Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David when they defied the Philistines who were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel had gone away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eleazar son of Dodai the Ahohite stood with David when the men of Israel withdrew. Arminian readers note his faithfulness when others fled.

1 Chronicles 11:12 gives his father’s name as Dodo, a spelling variant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see loyalty to the LORD’s anointed in a dangerous moment.

The narrator stresses that Eleazar stood when “the men of Israel had gone away.”

verses.text: He arose and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand froze to the sword; and the LORD worked a great victory that day; and the people returned after him only to take plunder.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eleazar fought until his hand froze to the sword, “and the LORD worked a great victory that day.” Arminian readers note that human effort and God’s action are held together.

The people returned only to collect the plunder.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the victory is credited to the LORD, even through Eleazar’s heroic effort.

Both traditions agree: God works through human courage, and the glory belongs to him.

verses.text: After him was Shammah the son of Agee, a Hararite. The Philistines had gathered together into a troop where there was a plot of ground full of lentils; and the people fled from the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shammah son of Agee defended a plot of lentils when the people fled. Arminian readers note another faithful stand against the odds.

1 Chronicles 11:13–14 describes a similar stand in a field of barley in its account of Eleazar; how the two accounts relate is a textual issue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s victory through faithful individuals.

The small plot becomes the scene of a great victory, showing that faithfulness in a small place matters.

verses.text: But he stood in the middle of the plot and defended it, and killed the Philistines; and the LORD worked a great victory.
verses.arminianNotes:
He stood in the middle of the plot, killed the Philistines, “and the LORD worked a great victory.” Arminian readers note the repetition of the phrase from verse 10.

Courage and divine help again go together.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same refrain crediting the LORD.

The narrator wants readers to see the heroes’ deeds as God’s work.

verses.text: Three of the thirty chief men went down, and came to David in the harvest time to the cave of Adullam; and the troop of the Philistines was encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
verses.arminianNotes:
Three of the thirty chief men come to David at the cave of Adullam during harvest, while the Philistines camp in the valley of Rephaim. Arminian readers note the setting in David’s fugitive years (cf. 1 Sam 22:1).

The story is placed here thematically rather than chronologically.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the loyalty of David’s men during a hard period.

The parallel account appears in 1 Chronicles 11:15–19.

verses.text: David was then in the stronghold; and the garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem.
verses.arminianNotes:
David is in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison is in Bethlehem. Arminian readers note the irony that David’s hometown is under enemy control.

The detail sets up his longing for its water.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the hardship of the anointed king not yet ruling his own land.

The situation makes the men’s deed all the more daring.

verses.text: David said longingly, “Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!”
verses.arminianNotes:
David longs for water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate. Arminian readers note the very human longing for home.

He does not command anyone to fetch it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see an expression of homesickness that his men take as an opportunity to show devotion.

The longing is honest, not a demand.

verses.text: The three mighty men broke through the army of the Philistines, and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David; but he would not drink of it, but poured it out to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The three break through the Philistine lines, draw water, and bring it to David, but he pours it out to the LORD. Arminian readers note David’s recognition that such a costly gift belongs to God.

The act honors both God and his men.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the water poured out as an offering, treating it as too precious for personal use.

Both traditions see reverence and gratitude in David’s response.

verses.text: He said, “Be it far from me, LORD, that I should do this! Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?” Therefore he would not drink it. The three mighty men did these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says, “Isn’t this the blood of the men who risked their lives to go?” and refuses to drink. Arminian readers note that he values his men’s lives above his own desire.

Leadership here means honoring sacrifice, not exploiting it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers connect the image of blood with life given to God (cf. Lev 17:11).

The scene shows a king who refuses to profit from others’ risk, a shared lesson for both traditions.
